newsitem.title: FRANCE: French president says state cannot do everything.
newsitem.headline: French president says state cannot do everything.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac believes that France can no longer rely on the state to keep rigid control of all aspects of the economy and that individual initiative is the force of the future.

"We have too long believed that the state alone can solve all problems. Modern economies require that the state stop trying to rigidly control everything," he wrote in an article due to appear on Sunday in the regional daily La Voix du Nord.

Chirac has previously called for an unspecified "third way" for Europe's economies -- somewhere between an economy driven purely by market forces and one tightly managed by the state. He has increasingly found the economic policies of his centre-right government under fire with the nation's jobless rate climbing to record levels.

He had pledged during his presidential election campaign last year to make job creation his top priority but later called instead for an austerity programme to bring down state deficits and help France qualify to participate in a planned European Union single currency from 1999.
France announced this week that its unemployment rate hit a record 12.6 percent in August.

Chirac discussed his economic beliefs in the paper ahead of a two-day trip to northern France beginning on Sunday. Aides said his visit would focus on stoking up the area economy through local, rather than national, initiatives.

Chirac telephoned a senior official of his Gaullist party this week to voice his indignation and make a plea for unity after Prime Minister Alain Juppe's policies came under heavy fire at a Gaullist conference.
Chirac's intervention was unusual because France's Fifth Republic constitution places the head of state above party politics.
Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin on Saturday accused the government of attempting to go forward "with its brakes locked" but put the blame on Chirac rather than Juppe.
"It is astonishing to see a president asking his deputies to spare the prime minister, because it was he (Chirac) who wrote the musical score," Jospin said in Narbonne in southeastern France.

Far-right politician Jean-Marie Le Pen commented on TF1 television that Juppe might end up with the support of 80 percent of his deputies, but added that "80 percent of the people will be against him".
